fetched_contents.text: Current knowledge and future research opportunities for modeling annual crop mixtures. A review | Agronomy for Sustainable Development Abstract Growing mixtures of annual arable crop species or genotypes is a promising way to improve crop production without increasing agricultural inputs. To design optimal crop mixtures, choices of species, genotypes, sowing proportion, plant arrangement, and sowing date need to be made but field experiments alone are not sufficient to explore such a large range of factors. Crop modeling allows to study, understand, and ultimately design cropping systems and is an established method for sole crops. Recently, modeling started to be applied to annual crop mixtures as well. Here, we review to what extent crop simulation models and individual-based models are suitable to capture and predict the specificities of annual crop mixtures. We argued that (1) the crop mixture spatio-temporal heterogeneity (influencing the occurrence of ecological processes) determines the choice of the modeling approach (plant or crop centered). (2) Only few crop models (adapted from sole crop models) and individual-based models currently exist to simulate annual crop mixtures. Crop models are mainly used to address issues related to both crop mixtures management and the integration of crop mixtures into larger scales such as the rotation. In contrast, individual-based models are mainly used to identify plant traits involved in crop mixture performance and to quantify the relative contribution of the different ecological processes (niche complementarity, facilitation, competition, plasticity) to crop mixture functioning. This review highlights that modeling of annual crop mixtures is in its infancy and gives to model users some important keys to choose the model based on the questions they want to answer, with awareness of the strengths and weaknesses of each of the modeling approaches. Similar content being viewed by others Acknowledgments References 1 Introduction The discipline of crop modeling emerged in the 1950s (Keating and Thorburn 2018) and is recognized as a crucial and operational tool to support improvement of cropping systems. One of its main strengths is that it enables multiple combinations of environments (climate and soil), genotypes, and agricultural practices to be explored and compared based on current knowledge of crop functioning in interaction with the environment (Bergez et al. 2010; Boote et al. 2013; Jeuffroy et al. 2014). A large scientific community supports crop modeling in international consortia, such as AgMIP (“Agricultural Model Intercomparison and Improvement Project”; Rosenzweig et al. 2013), to develop, improve, and evaluate models. For mainstream sole cropping systems (i.e., one genotype), crop modeling has been used to identify factors that limit crop productivity (e.g., Brisson et al. 2010), assess environmental impacts of crops (e.g., Liu et al. 2016), decrease inputs through improved management decisions (e.g., maize crop irrigation, Bergez et al. 2001; wheat fertilization, Chatelin et al. 2005), and aid breeding of new cultivars (reviewed by Chenu et al. 2017). At the field scale, sole crops are relatively homogeneous, especially when external inputs are used. Currently, crop modeling is facing challenges because the agroecological transition involves changes in agricultural practices (higher plant diversity, lower inputs, less tillage, biological regulation, tolerating residual weeds, etc.), which result in agroecosystems with greater complexity. Increasing public concerns about human and environmental health issues related to intensive agricultural systems over the past 70 years in Western industrialized countries have prompted policy makers and scientists to search for alternative management strategies, such as more diversified cropping systems (Duru et al. 2015). Increasing plant diversity in agriculture is suggested as a pathway towards more resilient and sustainable production systems (Lin 2011; Altieri et al. 2015; Raseduzzaman and Jensen 2017). At the farm scale, diversification can occur by diversifying crops in rotations (Gliessman 2014; Reckling 2016) and integrating agroecological pest (i.e., any organism harmful for crops) management to decrease pesticide use at farm and landscape scales (Lechenet et al. 2017; Hatt et al. 2018). At the field scale, plant diversity can increase using within-field mixtures of at least two annual crop species (i.e., intercropping; Fig. 1; Vandermeer 1989) or genotypes of the same species, both hereafter referred to as “annual crop mixtures.” Studies have demonstrated advantages of annual crop mixtures compared to their corresponding sole crops (reviewed by Lithourgidis et al. 2011; Bedoussac et al. 2015; Brooker et al. 2015; Li-li et al. 2015 for species diversity and Zeller et al. 2012; Creissen et al. 2016; Barot et al. 2017 for genotype diversity). Recent reviews and meta-analyses summarized the main ecosystem services they can deliver (Kiaer et al. 2009; Malézieux et al. 2009; Kremen and Miles 2012; Ehrmann and Ritz 2014; Altieri et al. 2015; Barot et al. 2017; Duchene et al. 2017; Raseduzzaman and Jensen 2017), highlighting their benefits for crop production (e.g., yield quality, quantity and stability), improvement of soil biogeochemistry (e.g., fertility, water flow regulation), improvement of biological pest control, and climate regulation by mitigating greenhouse gas emissions. Despite the potential of annual crop mixtures, they are under-represented in modern agriculture (Machado 2009; Costanzo and Bàrberi 2014). Like for sole crops, modeling could provide management guidelines to promote and optimize their use. fetched_contents.text: Characteristics of Grasses, Legumes, and other Forbs | Forage Information System Members of the grass family usually do not develop woody tissue, and die down at the end of a growing season. Grasses are monocotyledonous, a characteristic that is the basis for the development of glyphosate herbicides. One leaf sprouts from the seed; grasses have jointed, slender, sheathed leaves. They can be large or small and have erect or spreading growth habit. In addition to forages, grasses are important soil conservation tools; some are used as biomass fuels. * Optimal growth temperature is an important species selection characteristic. Grasses are classified into cool-season and warm-season types, with optimal growth temperature being 22° and 30° C (72° and 86° F), respectively. * Another important characteristic of grasses is their regrowth habit: culmed or culmless. Culmed types raise their apical meristem (growing points) during each regrowth cycle, making them more susceptible to ill-timed defoliation and typically less well suited to grazing. By contrast, culmless types have only leaf material in regrowth cycles. See Grass Growth and Regrowth for Improved Management for additional information. Legumes bear pods containing one or many seeds that are released from the pod as it ruptures. Leguminous plant roots host nodule-forming bacteria that can fix atmospheric nitrogen into plant-available nitrogen. Whether used as a forage or a seed, legumes are a source of protein-rich food. Legumes are useful cover and green manure crops, improve soil structure, and improve forage quality when seeded with grasses. Legumes have a narrower range of soil suitability conditions than grasses, in part because of the conditions required by the nodule-forming bacteria. As with grasses, legumes are grouped into cool-season and warm-season types based on their optimal growth temperature. Forbs are herbaceous, broadleaf plants. All legumes are forbs, but not all forbs are legumes. Species from several plant families are used for forage, with the mustards, and the cabbage family prominently represented. In recent decades, plantain (Plantago lanceolata L.) and chicory (Cichorium intybus L.) have gained popularity in pasture mixes (Labreveux et al., 2006). Forbs add diversity to pastures; once animals become accustomed to them, they are consumed readily. Some are deep-rooted and absorb minerals in different proportions than grasses and legumes.

These dynamics are challenging for land cover classifications on the one hand, but deliver crucial information that can be used to improve the classifiers performance on the other hand. Since up to date mapping of crops is crucial to assess the impact of agricultural land use on the ecosystems, an accurate and complete classification of crop types is of high importance. In the presented study, a new multitemporal data based classification approach was developed that incorporates knowledge about the phenological changes on crop lands. It identifies phenological sequence patterns (PSP) of the crop types based on a dense stack of Sentinel-1 data and accurate information about the plant's phenology. The performance of the developed methodology has been tested for two different vegetation seasons using over 200 ground truth fields located in northern Germany. The results showed that a dense time series of Sentinel-1 images allowed for high classification accuracies of grasslands, maize, canola, sugar beets and potatoes (F1-score above 0.8) using PSP as well as standard (Random Forest and Maximum Likelihood) classification method. The PSP approach clearly outperformed standard methods for cereal crops, especially for spring barley where the F1-score varied between zero and 0.43 for standard approaches, while PSP achieved values as high as 0.74 and 0.79 for both vegetation seasons. The PSP based approach also outperformed for oat, winter barley and rye. Furthermore, the PSP classification is more resilient to differences in farming management and conditions of growth since it takes information about each crop types' growing stage and its growing period into consideration. The results also indicate, that the PSP approach was more sensitive to subtle changes such as the proportion of weeds within a field. Keywords Agriculture ; Sentinel-1 ; Radar ; Classification ; Phenology Introduction The ongoing worldwide population growth is constantly increasing the demand of foods (FAO, 2007). This consequently results in the intensification of agricultural productions. The increased food production threatens those services provided by the ecosystems, also referred to as ecosystem services, that go beyond the production of food (Foley et al., 2005). Such an overstraining of supporting or regulating ecosystem services leads to the loss of e.g. fresh water or fertile soils or to negative changes in climate regulation (Foley et al., 2005, Poh Sze Choo et al., 2005, Tivy, 1993, Matson et al., 1997). Therefore, it is an indispensable premise to keep all services provided by the ecosystems in balance in order to avoid a collapse of the ecosystem services. For this purpose, decision makers, scientists and planners rely on detailed spatial information about the land cover in agricultural areas (Poh Sze Choo et al., 2005, Adamowicz et al., 2005, Feng et al., 2010). Since agricultural land is strongly affected by spatial and temporal dynamics within and between each vegetation season, the mapping of crops represents an especially challenging task. Thanks to regular revisiting intervals and weather independent acquisition capabilities, satellite-based imaging radar is well suited to capture the agricultural land use dynamics for crop mapping. This is shown by a large number of studies using a stack of radar images for multi-temporal classification approaches (McNairn et al., 2002, McNairn et al., 2009b, Bargiel and Herrmann, 2011, Bargiel, 2013, Sonobe et al., 2014, Skriver et al., 2011, Skriver, 2012, Larra naga and Álvarez Mozos, 2016, Mascolo et al., 2016, Larra naga and Álvarez Mozos, 2016). Sentinel-1 is a modern C-band imaging radar two satellite constellation, which was launched in 2014 and 2016 for earth observation. It is representing the first sensor designed for the Copernicus Project initiated by the European Union. It provides free data access and unprecedented high temporal resolution, which enables new possibilities to capture the dynamics in agricultural areas using multi-temporal classification approaches that include information about the crops' phenology. In contrary to most land cover types, agricultural areas vary strongly within very short time intervals. Most crop types' have a vegetation period of several months. In this time, the plants phenology changes strongly many times between seeding and harvest. Furthermore, the life cycles beginnings and endings differ depending on the crop types (cf. Fig. 1). This is also true for the different stages within the plant's phenological development, for instance germination, leaf development or flowering as illustrated in Fig. 1. Further dynamics take place during the time intervals before the seeding period (preparation) and after the harvest (post harvest). During this time, the areas are affected by deviating management of the farmers. This is not necessarily unique depending on the types of crops that are planning to be planted or have been harvested. In summary, there are two types of short-term changes: the crop-type specific changes occurring between seeding and harvest (within the life cycle) and the non-crop-type specific differences outside the life cycle depending on the farmers management. Branch report on morphological classification of annual crop mixtures

The classification of annual crop mixtures by morphology is built around the idea that mixtures are distinguished by the physical differences among their component species or genotypes. The evidence here identifies morphological heterogeneity as a key dimension of crop mixture classification, with the review explicitly stating that crop mixtures “meet morphological and phenological heterogeneity requirements for harvest” and that classification is based on a “double gradient of phenological and morphological heterogeneities” [N1-R1][N1-F1]. This means morphology is treated as a primary organizing principle, not just a secondary trait.

Commonly used morphological traits include plant height, canopy structure, and root architecture, all of which are directly relevant to how mixtures are structured and interpreted. The evidence also notes that plant height and canopy structure are part of the broader morphological heterogeneity framework, while root architecture is tied to the ecological functioning of mixtures [N1-R2]. In practical terms, this means classification systems often look at how tall or short species are, how they shade the field, and how their root systems occupy space belowground.

Legumes, cereals, and grasses differ markedly in morphology. Grasses are monocotyledonous plants with jointed, slender, sheathed leaves, and they can have erect or spreading growth habits [N2-F2]. They are typically categorized by growth temperature into cool-season and warm-season types, and by regrowth habit into culmed or culmless types [N2-F2]. Legumes, in contrast, bear pods containing one or many seeds and have roots that host nodule-forming bacteria that fix atmospheric nitrogen [N2-F2]. Legumes are also described as protein-rich forage plants and as useful cover and green manure crops, which helps explain why they are often grouped with grasses in mixtures [N2-F2]. Forbs are herbaceous, broadleaf plants that are not necessarily legumes, and they can add diversity and have deep roots that absorb minerals differently than grasses and legumes [N2-F2]. These differences make morphology a natural basis for classification: mixtures are often grouped by whether they include grasses, legumes, and/or forbs, because these groups have distinct visual and structural profiles.

Plant height contributes directly to classification because taller species shade shorter ones and alter the vertical structure of the canopy [N1-R2]. Canopy structure matters because it affects light capture, competition, and the spatial arrangement of the mixture [N1-R2]. Root architecture is also operationalized in classification because it influences resource capture and how species interact belowground [N1-R2]. The evidence indicates that these traits are used together in practical mixture design: mixtures are chosen and arranged by species, genotype, sowing proportion, and plant arrangement, with morphology and phenology both shaping how they perform [N1-F1]. So, morphological classification is not just about identifying species; it is about understanding how their physical differences create different mixture architectures and competitive dynamics.

In short, morphological classification of annual crop mixtures relies on traits such as plant height, canopy structure, and root architecture, with legumes, cereals, grasses, and forbs distinguished by leaf form, growth habit, nitrogen fixation, and rooting behavior [N1-R1][N1-F1][N2-F2]. These traits help define mixtures and explain why certain combinations are selected for agronomic purposes.

Branch report on phenological classification of annual crop mixtures

Phenological classification of annual crop mixtures is centered on the idea that mixtures differ by the timing of their life cycle events. The evidence explicitly states that phenological traits include growth duration, days to maturity, days from emergence to flowering, and harvesting time, while morphological traits are also part of the broader heterogeneity framework [N1-R2]. The same source also notes that classification is based on a double gradient of phenological and morphological heterogeneities, reinforcing that phenology is not treated as an isolated attribute but as part of a larger classification logic [N1-R1][N1-F1].

Common phenological traits used to classify mixtures include emergence timing, flowering timing, and maturity timing. These are clearly operationalized as important phenological characteristics in the evidence: growth duration, days to maturity, days required from emergence to flowering, and harvesting time are all cited as phenological traits [N1-R2]. A separate source on phenological phases adds that phenological phases are stages in a plant’s life cycle and development, such as budding, flowering, fruit set, and ripening [N3-F3]. This supports the view that phenological classification is about how species unfold over time rather than just their static form.

Emergence, flowering, and maturity timing differ among mixture components in ways that shape classification. The evidence indicates that phenological differences can create distinct developmental sequences within a mixture [N1-R2]. For example, some species may emerge earlier, flower later, and mature more quickly than others, which can affect how they compete for resources and how the mixture is managed [N1-R2]. The phenology-based classification approach described in the search result also highlights that phenology is used to identify crop types based on phenological and spectral metrics, showing that temporal differentiation is a central classification criterion [N5-R5]. In practice, this means that mixtures are often categorized by whether components have overlapping or staggered phenological patterns, and by the length of their growth cycles [N1-R2][N3-F3].

Temporal niche and resource capture are closely related to phenological classification because the timing of life cycle events determines when plants capture sunlight, water, and nutrients. The evidence states that growing degree day models for spring phenology depend on the species’ temporal niche, and that satellite-derived crop phenology can improve classification by capturing temporal changes during the agricultural cycle [N5-R3][N5-R4]. This implies that phenological classification is not only about identifying species but also about understanding how they occupy different temporal niches and how those niches affect resource use. A mixture with components that flower and mature at different times can therefore be classified as having a broader temporal niche, which may improve resource capture and reduce competition [N5-R3][N5-R4].

In sum, phenological classification of annual crop mixtures is based on traits such as emergence timing, flowering timing, maturity timing, and growth duration, with components distinguished by their phenological sequences and temporal niches [N1-R2][N3-F3][N5-R3]. These traits are operationalized as the basis for identifying mixtures and for understanding how they capture resources over time [N5-R4]. The evidence also shows that phenological classification is increasingly linked to remote sensing and model-based approaches that use time series data to improve accuracy [N5-R4][N5-R5].

Branch report on performance and practical implications of classification

Morphology and phenology jointly predict competition and yield by shaping how species occupy space and time. The evidence indicates that crop mixtures are classified based on a double gradient of phenological and morphological heterogeneity, which is directly tied to mixture functioning [N1-R1][N1-F1]. Morphological differences such as plant height, canopy structure, and root architecture influence competition by altering light interception, resource capture, and root-space occupation [N1-R2]. Phenological differences such as emergence, flowering, maturity timing, and growth duration determine how species interact temporally, affecting resource availability and competition intensity [N1-R2][N3-F3]. Together, these traits are used to identify plant traits involved in crop mixture performance and to quantify the relative contribution of niche complementarity, facilitation, competition, and plasticity [N1-F1]. In other words, classification is not only a taxonomy; it is a way of understanding why mixtures may outperform monocultures.

The evidence also shows that certain mixture types are associated with greater stability or productivity. Wheat mixtures demonstrated both mid-component and better-component overyielding, with stronger effects under low-input conditions [N4-R1]. Cultivar mixtures increased crop yields and temporal yield stability globally, and varietal mixtures stabilized productivity even when environmental conditions and stresses were not predicted [N4-R2][N4-R3]. A meta-analysis also found that cultivar mixtures improved resource-use efficiency and reduced disease severity [N4-R2]. These results suggest that mixtures with more heterogeneity can be more stable and productive, especially in stressful or variable conditions. The evidence further indicates that multifaceted functional diversity improves multifaceted crop yield, reinforcing the idea that mixture composition matters for both biomass and grain yield [N4-R4]. However, the evidence also notes that performance depends on the specific combination and arrangement of species, genotypes, and management practices [N1-F1], so classification systems must account for more than just species identity.

Classification systems are used in agronomy and farm practice to design mixtures, manage them, and integrate them into larger scales. The review states that crop modeling is used to address issues related to both crop mixture management and the integration of mixtures into larger scales such as rotation [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that modeling helps identify plant traits involved in mixture performance and quantify ecological processes [N1-F1]. This means classification systems are operationalized in practice through decisions about species selection, sowing proportion, plant arrangement, sowing date, and management timing [N1-F1]. The evidence on crop classification also shows that phenological information improves remote sensing-based classification, and that temporal changes in crop phenology help achieve better classifications [N5-R4][N5-R5]. This implies that farmers and agronomists use classification systems not only to identify mixtures but also to schedule planting, harvesting, and interventions more effectively.

Overall, the evidence supports a practical conclusion: morphology and phenology are jointly predictive of competition and yield because they determine how species occupy space and time [N1-R2][N3-F3]. Mixture types with greater heterogeneity, such as wheat mixtures and cultivar mixtures, are often associated with greater stability and productivity, especially under low-input or unpredictable conditions [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3]. Classification systems are used in agronomy to design, manage, and optimize mixtures, and they are increasingly supported by modeling and remote sensing approaches that integrate phenological and morphological information [N1-F1][N5-R4][N5-R5].

Branch report on classification systems and terminology

Different sources define or classify crop mixtures using a combination of functional, structural, and temporal criteria. The evidence indicates that mixtures are often distinguished from intercropping and cultivar mixtures by the scale of diversity and the units of analysis. The review states that “within-field mixtures of at least two annual crop species” are referred to as “annual crop mixtures,” whereas “genotypes of the same species” are also included in this category [N1-F1]. This is important because it shows that classification systems must distinguish between species mixtures and genotype mixtures, even though both are called “mixtures.” The evidence also notes that mixture effects are broadly classified as phenological and morphological heterogeneity of cereal and legume intercropping [N7-R2], suggesting that some sources use intercropping terminology more broadly than a strict definition would allow.

Terminology distinguishes mixtures, intercropping, and cultivar mixtures by the level of diversity and the units being mixed. The review explicitly defines annual crop mixtures as within-field mixtures of at least two annual crop species, or genotypes of the same species [N1-F1]. That definition implies that intercropping is a broader concept that can include multiple species and genotypes, but the review itself uses “annual crop mixtures” as the more precise term for within-field mixtures of species or genotypes [N1-F1]. Cultivar mixtures are also mentioned in the evidence as a separate category of mixtures, and the source states that cultivar mixtures are part of the broader framework of annual crop mixtures [N7-R2]. This terminology distinction matters because it affects how mixtures are classified: species-level mixtures versus genotype-level mixtures, and whether the mixture is defined by species, cultivars, or both.

Morphological/phenological heterogeneity is operationalized in classification through explicit traits and sequences. The evidence shows that morphological heterogeneity is tied to plant height, canopy structure, and root architecture [N1-R2]. Phenological heterogeneity is operationalized through emergence timing, flowering timing, maturity timing, growth duration, and other phenological phases [N1-R2][N3-F3]. The review also states that classification is based on a double gradient of phenological and morphological heterogeneity, which means that both traits are used together to define mixtures and evaluate their functioning [N1-R1][N1-F1]. In addition, remote sensing and modeling approaches explicitly use phenological information to improve crop classification, and phenology-based methods are used to identify crop types [N5-R4][N5-R5]. This operationalization shows that classification systems are not purely taxonomic; they are performance-oriented frameworks that incorporate observable and measurable traits.

The broader classification literature also emphasizes that different sources may use terminology differently. The evidence includes a source discussing landscape heterogeneity and crop classification accuracy [N7-R1], and another on automatic crop classification using spectral-temporal profiles and phenological information [N7-R4]. These sources support the idea that classification systems can be based on a variety of features, including spatial heterogeneity, spectral information, and phenological sequences [N7-R1][N7-R4]. The source on cultivars further clarifies that homogeneity and heterogeneity refer to genetic and phenotypic relationships among plants in a cultivar, and that a cultivar is homogeneous by definition [N7-R5]. This helps distinguish cultivar mixtures from species mixtures: the former may be homogeneous at the cultivar level but heterogeneous at the mixture level, whereas the latter is defined by species-level diversity [N7-R5].

In conclusion, different sources define crop mixtures by whether they are within-field mixtures of species or genotypes, and by whether they are called mixtures, intercropping, or cultivar mixtures [N1-F1][N7-R2]. Morphological/phenological heterogeneity is operationalized through traits such as plant height, canopy structure, root architecture, emergence timing, flowering timing, maturity timing, and phenological phases [N1-R2][N3-F3]. Classification systems are increasingly supported by remote sensing and modeling approaches that integrate phenological and morphological information [N5-R4][N5-R5]. The terminology distinction is important because it affects how mixtures are interpreted and managed in agronomy.

# How annual crop mixtures are classified by morphological and phenological heterogeneity

Annual crop mixtures are classified by morphology and phenology because these traits define how species occupy space and time, how they compete, and how they can be managed. The evidence consistently portrays classification as a double gradient of **phenological and morphological heterogeneity**, meaning mixtures are distinguished not only by species identity but also by how they differ in life-cycle timing and physical structure [N1-R1][N1-F1]. This classification logic is operationalized in practice through observable traits and is increasingly supported by crop modeling and remote-sensing approaches that use phenological and morphological information [N1-F1][N5-R4][N5-R5].

## 1) Morphological classification: traits, species differences, and functional structure

Morphological classification centers on the physical differences among mixture components. The evidence identifies commonly used traits such as **plant height, canopy structure, and root architecture** as central to classification [N1-R2]. These traits are important because they influence how plants shade one another, how they capture light and nutrients, and how they occupy the soil belowground [N1-R2].

Legumes, cereals, grasses, and forbs differ in morphology in ways that make them readily distinguishable in mixtures. Grasses are monocotyledonous plants with **jointed, slender, sheathed leaves**, and they can have **erect or spreading growth habits** [N2-F2]. They are also classified by growth temperature into **cool-season and warm-season** types, and by regrowth habit into **culmed or culmless** types [N2-F2]. Legumes, by contrast, bear **pods containing one or many seeds** and have **nodule-forming bacteria** on their roots that can fix atmospheric nitrogen [N2-F2]. Legumes are described as **protein-rich forage plants** and useful as **cover and green manure crops**, which explains why they are often grouped with grasses in mixtures [N2-F2]. Forbs are **herbaceous, broadleaf plants**, not all of which are legumes, and they can add diversity and have **deep roots** that absorb minerals differently than grasses and legumes [N2-F2].

These morphological differences matter for classification because they create different mixture architectures. Taller species can shade shorter ones, altering light capture and competition; dense canopies can change resource distribution; and different root systems can affect nutrient cycling and belowground competition [N1-R2]. The evidence also shows that morphology is used in practical mixture design, with decisions about **species, genotype, sowing proportion, plant arrangement, and sowing date** shaping the final mixture [N1-F1].

## 2) Phenological classification: timing, sequences, and temporal niches

Phenological classification is based on the timing of life-cycle events. The evidence explicitly identifies **emergence timing, flowering timing, maturity timing, growth duration, and harvesting time** as key phenological traits [N1-R2]. It also notes that phenological phases are **stages in a plant’s life cycle and development**, such as **budding, flowering, fruit set, and ripening** [N3-F3]. This means phenological classification is about how species unfold over time, not just their static form.

In mixtures, emergence, flowering, and maturity timing differ among components. Some species may **emerge earlier, flower later, and mature more quickly** than others, creating distinct developmental sequences within the mixture [N1-R2]. The evidence also links phenological classification to **temporal niche**, showing that species with different phenological sequences occupy different parts of the growing season and can therefore reduce competition [N5-R3]. This is important because resource capture depends on when plants are active: sunlight, water, and nutrients are captured at different times by different species [N5-R3][N5-R4].

Phenological classification is further supported by remote sensing and model-based approaches. The evidence shows that **satellite-derived crop phenology** can improve classification, and that **phenology-based methods** are used to identify crop types [N5-R4][N5-R5]. These approaches emphasize that phenological information is not just descriptive; it is predictive and operational. A mixture with components that flower and mature at different times can therefore be classified as having a broader temporal niche, which may improve resource capture and reduce competition [N5-R3][N5-R4].

## 3) Classification systems and terminology: definitions and operationalization

Different sources define crop mixtures in subtly different ways, which is important for classification. The evidence indicates that **annual crop mixtures** are defined as **within-field mixtures of at least two annual crop species**, or **genotypes of the same species** [N1-F1]. This distinction matters because it separates **species-level mixtures** from **genotype-level mixtures**. It also shows that the term “mixtures” can encompass both **intercropping** and **cultivar mixtures**, although the review itself uses “annual crop mixtures” as the more precise category [N1-F1][N7-R2].

Terminology helps distinguish the three main concepts:
- **Mixtures** refer broadly to combinations of species or genotypes in the field [N1-F1].
- **Intercropping** is used more generally in some sources, but the evidence frames “annual crop mixtures” as the preferred term for within-field mixtures of species or genotypes [N1-F1][N7-R2].
- **Cultivar mixtures** are a subset of mixtures, referring to combinations of genotypes within a species [N7-R2].

Morphological and phenological heterogeneity is operationalized in classification through explicit traits and sequences. Morphological heterogeneity is tied to **plant height, canopy structure, and root architecture** [N1-R2], while phenological heterogeneity is tied to **emergence timing, flowering timing, maturity timing, growth duration, and phenological phases** [N1-R2][N3-F3]. The evidence also shows that classification is based on a **double gradient** of phenological and morphological heterogeneity [N1-R1][N1-F1]. In other words, mixtures are not classified by a single trait alone; they are classified by how their components differ in both form and timing.

This operationalization is increasingly supported by remote sensing and modeling. The evidence shows that crop classification can be improved by integrating **phenological information** and that **phenology-based approaches** are used to identify crop types [N5-R4][N5-R5]. It also notes that landscape heterogeneity and spectral-temporal profiles are used in crop classification systems, showing that classification is not only taxonomic but also performance-oriented [N7-R1][N7-R4]. The cultivar-related evidence further clarifies that **homogeneity and heterogeneity** refer to genetic and phenotypic relationships among plants in a cultivar, and that a cultivar is homogeneous by definition [N7-R5]. This helps distinguish cultivar mixtures from species mixtures: the former may be homogeneous at the cultivar level but heterogeneous at the mixture level, whereas the latter is defined by species-level diversity [N7-R5].

## 4) Performance and practical implications

Morphology and phenology jointly predict competition and yield by shaping how species occupy space and time. The evidence states that crop mixtures are classified based on a **double gradient of phenological and morphological heterogeneity**, which is directly tied to mixture functioning [N1-R1][N1-F1]. Morphological differences such as plant height, canopy structure, and root architecture influence competition by altering **light interception, resource capture, and root-space occupation** [N1-R2]. Phenological differences such as emergence, flowering, maturity timing, and growth duration determine how species interact temporally, affecting **resource availability and competition intensity** [N1-R2][N3-F3]. Together, these traits are used to identify plant traits involved in mixture performance and to quantify the relative contribution of **niche complementarity, facilitation, competition, and plasticity** [N1-F1].

The evidence also shows that certain mixture types are associated with greater stability or productivity. **Wheat mixtures** demonstrated both mid-component and better-component overyielding, with stronger effects under low-input conditions [N4-R1]. **Cultivar mixtures** increased crop yields and temporal yield stability globally, and **varietal mixtures** stabilized productivity even when environmental conditions and stresses were not predicted [N4-R2][N4-R3]. A meta-analysis found that cultivar mixtures improved **resource-use efficiency** and reduced **disease severity** [N4-R2]. The evidence further indicates that **multifaceted functional diversity** improves multifaceted crop yield, reinforcing the idea that mixture composition matters for both **biomass and grain yield** [N4-R4]. However, the evidence also notes that performance depends on the specific combination and arrangement of species, genotypes, and management practices [N1-F1], so classification systems must account for more than just species identity.

In agronomy and farm practice, classification systems are used to **design mixtures, manage them, and integrate them into larger scales**. The review states that crop modeling is used to address issues related to both **crop mixture management** and the **integration of mixtures into larger scales such as rotation** [N1-F1]. Branch report on morphological classification of annual crop mixtures

The classification of annual crop mixtures by morphology is built around the idea that mixtures are distinguished by the physical differences among their component species or genotypes. The evidence here identifies morphological heterogeneity as a key dimension of crop mixture classification, with the review explicitly stating that crop mixtures “meet morphological and phenological heterogeneity requirements for harvest” and that classification is based on a “double gradient of phenological and morphological heterogeneities” [N1-R1][N1-F1]. This means morphology is treated as a primary organizing principle, not just a secondary trait.

Commonly used morphological traits include plant height, canopy structure, and root architecture, all of which are directly relevant to how mixtures are structured and interpreted. The evidence also notes that plant height and canopy structure are part of the broader morphological heterogeneity framework, while root architecture is tied to the ecological functioning of mixtures [N1-R2]. In practical terms, this means classification systems often look at how tall or short species are, how they shade the field, and how their root systems occupy space belowground.

Legumes, cereals, and grasses differ markedly in morphology. Grasses are monocotyledonous plants with jointed, slender, sheathed leaves, and they can have erect or spreading growth habits [N2-F2]. They are typically categorized by growth temperature into cool-season and warm-season types, and by regrowth habit into culmed or culmless types [N2-F2]. Legumes, in contrast, bear pods containing one or many seeds and have roots that host nodule-forming bacteria that fix atmospheric nitrogen [N2-F2]. Legumes are also described as protein-rich forage plants and as useful cover and green manure crops, which helps explain why they are often grouped with grasses in mixtures [N2-F2]. Forbs are herbaceous, broadleaf plants that are not necessarily legumes, and they can add diversity and have deep roots that absorb minerals differently than grasses and legumes [N2-F2]. These differences make morphology a natural basis for classification: mixtures are often grouped by whether they include grasses, legumes, and/or forbs, because these groups have distinct visual and structural profiles.

Plant height contributes directly to classification because taller species shade shorter ones and alter the vertical structure of the canopy [N1-R2]. Canopy structure matters because it affects light capture, competition, and the spatial arrangement of the mixture [N1-R2]. Root architecture is also operationalized in classification because it influences resource capture and how species interact belowground [N1-R2]. The evidence indicates that these traits are used together in practical mixture design: mixtures are chosen and arranged by species, genotype, sowing proportion, and plant arrangement, with morphology and phenology both shaping how they perform [N1-F1]. So, morphological classification is not just about identifying species; it is about understanding how their physical differences create different mixture architectures and competitive dynamics.

In short, morphological classification of annual crop mixtures relies on traits such as plant height, canopy structure, and root architecture, with legumes, cereals, grasses, and forbs distinguished by leaf form, growth habit, nitrogen fixation, and rooting behavior [N1-R1][N1-F1][N2-F2]. These traits help define mixtures and explain why certain combinations are selected for agronomic purposes.

# How annual crop mixtures are classified by morphological and phenological heterogeneity

Annual crop mixtures are classified by morphology and phenology because these traits define how species occupy space and time, how they compete, and how they can be managed. The evidence consistently portrays classification as a double gradient of **phenological and morphological heterogeneity**, meaning mixtures are distinguished not only by species identity but also by how they differ in life-cycle timing and physical structure [N1-R1][N1-F1]. This classification logic is operationalized in practice through observable traits and is increasingly supported by crop modeling and remote-sensing approaches that use phenological and morphological information [N1-F1][N5-R4][N5-R5].

## 1) Morphological classification: traits, species differences, and functional structure

Morphological classification centers on the physical differences among mixture components. The evidence identifies commonly used traits such as **plant height, canopy structure, and root architecture** as central to classification [N1-R2]. These traits are important because they influence how plants shade one another, how they capture light and nutrients, and how they occupy the soil belowground [N1-R2].

Legumes, cereals, grasses, and forbs differ in morphology in ways that make them readily distinguishable in mixtures. Grasses are monocotyledonous plants with **jointed, slender, sheathed leaves**, and they can have **erect or spreading growth habits** [N2-F2]. They are also classified by growth temperature into **cool-season and warm-season** types, and by regrowth habit into **culmed or culmless** types [N2-F2]. Legumes, by contrast, bear **pods containing one or many seeds** and have **nodule-forming bacteria** on their roots that can fix atmospheric nitrogen [N2-F2]. Legumes are described as **protein-rich forage plants** and useful as **cover and green manure crops**, which explains why they are often grouped with grasses in mixtures [N2-F2]. Forbs are **herbaceous, broadleaf plants**, not all of which are legumes, and they can add diversity and have **deep roots** that absorb minerals differently than grasses and legumes [N2-F2].

These morphological differences matter for classification because they create different mixture architectures. Taller species can shade shorter ones, altering light capture and competition; dense canopies can change resource distribution; and different root systems can affect nutrient cycling and belowground competition [N1-R2]. The evidence also shows that morphology is used in practical mixture design, with decisions about **species, genotype, sowing proportion, plant arrangement, and sowing date** shaping the final mixture [N1-F1].

## 2) Phenological classification: timing, sequences, and temporal niches

Phenological classification is based on the timing of life-cycle events. The evidence explicitly identifies **emergence timing, flowering timing, maturity timing, growth duration, and harvesting time** as key phenological traits [N1-R2]. It also notes that phenological phases are **stages in a plant’s life cycle and development**, such as **budding, flowering, fruit set, and ripening** [N3-F3]. This means phenological classification is about how species unfold over time, not just their static form.

In mixtures, emergence, flowering, and maturity timing differ among components. Some species may **emerge earlier, flower later, and mature more quickly** than others, creating distinct developmental sequences within the mixture [N1-R2]. The evidence also links phenological classification to **temporal niche**, showing that species with different phenological sequences occupy different parts of the growing season and can therefore reduce competition [N5-R3]. This is important because resource capture depends on when plants are active: sunlight, water, and nutrients are captured at different times by different species [N5-R3][N5-R4].

Phenological classification is further supported by remote sensing and model-based approaches. The evidence shows that **satellite-derived crop phenology** can improve classification, and that **phenology-based methods** are used to identify crop types [N5-R4][N5-R5]. These approaches emphasize that phenological information is not just descriptive; it is predictive and operational. A mixture with components that flower and mature at different times can therefore be classified as having a broader temporal niche, which may improve resource capture and reduce competition [N5-R3][N5-R4].

## 3) Classification systems and terminology: definitions and operationalization

Different sources define crop mixtures in subtly different ways, which is important for classification. The evidence indicates that **annual crop mixtures** are defined as **within-field mixtures of at least two annual crop species**, or **genotypes of the same species** [N1-F1]. This distinction matters because it separates **species-level mixtures** from **genotype-level mixtures**. It also shows that the term “mixtures” can encompass both **intercropping** and **cultivar mixtures**, although the review itself uses “annual crop mixtures” as the more precise category [N1-F1][N7-R2].

Terminology helps distinguish the three main concepts:
- **Mixtures** refer broadly to combinations of species or genotypes in the field [N1-F1].
- **Intercropping** is used more generally in some sources, but the evidence frames “annual crop mixtures” as the preferred term for within-field mixtures of species or genotypes [N1-F1][N7-R2].
- **Cultivar mixtures** are a subset of mixtures, referring to combinations of genotypes within a species [N7-R2].

Morphological and phenological heterogeneity is operationalized in classification through explicit traits and sequences. Morphological heterogeneity is tied to **plant height, canopy structure, and root architecture** [N1-R2], while phenological heterogeneity is tied to **emergence timing, flowering timing, maturity timing, growth duration, and phenological phases** [N1-R2][N3-F3]. The evidence also shows that classification is based on a **double gradient** of phenological and morphological heterogeneity [N1-R1][N1-F1]. In other words, mixtures are not classified by a single trait alone; they are classified by how their components differ in both form and timing.

This operationalization is increasingly supported by remote sensing and modeling. The evidence shows that crop classification can be improved by integrating **phenological information** and that **phenology-based approaches** are used to identify crop types [N5-R4][N5-R5]. It also notes that landscape heterogeneity and spectral-temporal profiles are used in crop classification systems, showing that classification is not only taxonomic but also performance-oriented [N7-R1][N7-R4]. The cultivar-related evidence further clarifies that **homogeneity and heterogeneity** refer to genetic and phenotypic relationships among plants in a cultivar, and that a cultivar is homogeneous by definition [N7-R5]. This helps distinguish cultivar mixtures from species mixtures: the former may be homogeneous at the cultivar level but heterogeneous at the mixture level, whereas the latter is defined by species-level diversity [N7-R5].

## 4) Performance and practical implications

Morphology and phenology jointly predict competition and yield by shaping how species occupy space and time. The evidence states that crop mixtures are classified based on a **double gradient of phenological and morphological heterogeneity**, which is directly tied to mixture functioning [N1-R1][N1-F1]. Morphological differences such as plant height, canopy structure, and root architecture influence competition by altering **light interception, resource capture, and root-space occupation** [N1-R2]. Phenological differences such as emergence, flowering, maturity timing, and growth duration determine how species interact temporally, affecting **resource availability and competition intensity** [N1-R2][N3-F3]. Together, these traits are used to identify plant traits involved in mixture performance and to quantify the relative contribution of **niche complementarity, facilitation, competition, and plasticity** [N1-F1].

The evidence also shows that certain mixture types are associated with greater stability or productivity. **Wheat mixtures** demonstrated both mid-component and better-component overyielding, with stronger effects under low-input conditions [N4-R1]. **Cultivar mixtures** increased crop yields and temporal yield stability globally, and **varietal mixtures** stabilized productivity even when environmental conditions and stresses were not predicted [N4-R2][N4-R3]. A meta-analysis found that cultivar mixtures improved **resource-use efficiency** and reduced **disease severity** [N4-R2]. The evidence further indicates that **multifaceted functional diversity** improves multifaceted crop yield, reinforcing the idea that mixture composition matters for both **biomass and grain yield** [N4-R4]. However, the evidence also notes that performance depends on the specific combination and arrangement of species, genotypes, and management practices [N1-F1], so classification systems must account for more than just species identity.

In agronomy and farm practice, classification systems are used to **design mixtures, manage them, and integrate them into larger scales**. The review states that crop modeling is used to address issues related to both **crop mixture management** and the **integration of mixtures into larger scales such as rotation** [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that modeling helps identify plant traits involved in mixture performance and quantify ecological processes [N1-F1]. This means classification systems are operationalized in practice through decisions about **species selection, sowing proportion, plant arrangement, sowing date, and management timing** [N1-F1]. The evidence on crop classification also shows that **phenological information improves remote sensing-based classification**, and that temporal changes in crop phenology help achieve better classifications [N5-R4][N5-R5]. This implies that farmers and agronomists use classification systems not only to identify mixtures but also to schedule planting, harvesting, and interventions more effectively [N5-R4][N5-R5].

## 5) Integrated conclusion

Annual crop mixtures are classified by morphological and phenological heterogeneity because these traits determine how species occupy space, compete, and capture resources over time. Morphological classification uses **plant height, canopy structure, and root architecture** to distinguish legumes, cereals, grasses, and forbs [N1-R2][N2-F2]. Phenological classification uses **emergence timing, flowering timing, maturity timing, growth duration, and phenological phases** to distinguish components by their temporal sequences [N1-R2][N3-F3]. These two dimensions are combined into a **double gradient of phenological and morphological heterogeneity**, which is the basis for mixture classification and performance analysis [N1-R1][N1-F1].

Classification systems are also shaped by terminology. Different sources define **mixtures**, **intercropping**, and **cultivar mixtures** differently, but the evidence supports a practical distinction between species-level mixtures and genotype-level mixtures [N1-F1][N7-R2]. Morphological and phenological heterogeneity are operationalized through observable traits and sequences, and they are increasingly supported by remote sensing and modeling approaches that integrate phenological and morphological information [N5-R4][N5-R5][N7-R1][N7-R4]. Finally, these classification systems have clear practical implications: mixtures with greater heterogeneity can be more stable and productive, especially under low-input or unpredictable conditions [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3]. In practice, this means classification is not just a taxonomy; it is a way of designing, managing, and optimizing crop mixtures for sustainable and resilient farming.

This classification logic is operationalized in practice through observable traits and is increasingly supported by crop modeling and remote-sensing approaches that use phenological and morphological information [N1-F1][N5-R4][N5-R5].

## 1) Morphological classification: traits, species differences, and functional structure

Morphological classification centers on the physical differences among mixture components. The evidence identifies commonly used traits such as **plant height, canopy structure, and root architecture** as central to classification [N1-R2]. These traits are important because they influence how plants shade one another, how they capture light and nutrients, and how they occupy the soil belowground [N1-R2].

Legumes, cereals, grasses, and forbs differ in morphology in ways that make them readily distinguishable in mixtures. Grasses are monocotyledonous plants with **jointed, slender, sheathed leaves**, and they can have **erect or spreading growth habits** [N2-F2]. They are also classified by growth temperature into **cool-season and warm-season** types, and by regrowth habit into **culmed or culmless** types [N2-F2]. Legumes, by contrast, bear **pods containing one or many seeds** and have **nodule-forming bacteria** on their roots that can fix atmospheric nitrogen [N2-F2]. Legumes are described as **protein-rich forage plants** and useful as **cover and green manure crops**, which explains why they are often grouped with grasses in mixtures [N2-F2]. Forbs are **herbaceous, broadleaf plants**, not all of which are legumes, and they can add diversity and have **deep roots** that absorb minerals differently than grasses and legumes [N2-F2].

These morphological differences matter for classification because they create different mixture architectures. Taller species can shade shorter ones, altering light capture and competition; dense canopies can change resource distribution; and different root systems can affect nutrient cycling and belowground competition [N1-R2]. The evidence also shows that morphology is used in practical mixture design, with decisions about **species, genotype, sowing proportion, plant arrangement, and sowing date** shaping the final mixture [N1-F1].

## 2) Phenological classification: timing, sequences, and temporal niches

Phenological classification is based on the timing of life-cycle events. The evidence explicitly identifies **emergence timing, flowering timing, maturity timing, growth duration, and harvesting time** as key phenological traits [N1-R2]. Different sources define crop mixtures in subtly different ways, which is important for classification. - **Intercropping** is used more generally in some sources, but the evidence frames “annual crop mixtures” as the preferred term for within-field mixtures of species or genotypes [N1-F1][N7-R2].

## 5) Integrated conclusion

Annual crop mixtures are classified by morphological and phenological heterogeneity because these traits determine how species occupy space, compete, and capture resources over time. Morphological classification uses **plant height, canopy structure, and root architecture** to distinguish legumes, cereals, grasses, and forbs [N1-R2][N2-F2]. # How annual crop mixtures are classified by morphological and phenological heterogeneity

Annual crop mixtures are classified by morphology and phenology because these traits define how species occupy space and time, how they compete, and how they can be managed. The evidence consistently portrays classification as a double gradient of **phenological and morphological heterogeneity**, meaning mixtures are distinguished not only by species identity but also by how they differ in life-cycle timing and physical structure [N1-R1][N1-F1]. This classification logic is operationalized in practice through observable traits and is increasingly supported by crop modeling and remote-sensing approaches that use phenological and morphological information [N1-F1][N5-R4][N5-R5].

## 1) Morphological classification: traits, species differences, and functional structure

Morphological classification centers on the physical differences among mixture components. The evidence identifies commonly used traits such as **plant height, canopy structure, and root architecture** as central to classification [N1-R2]. These traits are important because they influence how plants shade one another, how they capture light and nutrients, and how they occupy the soil belowground [N1-R2].

Legumes, cereals, grasses, and forbs differ in morphology in ways that make them readily distinguishable in mixtures. Grasses are monocotyledonous plants with **jointed, slender, sheathed leaves**, and they can have **erect or spreading growth habits** [N2-F2]. They are also classified by growth temperature into **cool-season and warm-season** types, and by regrowth habit into **culmed or culmless** types [N2-F2]. Legumes, by contrast, bear **pods containing one or many seeds** and have **nodule-forming bacteria** on their roots that can fix atmospheric nitrogen [N2-F2]. Legumes are described as **protein-rich forage plants** and useful as **cover and green manure crops**, which explains why they are often grouped with grasses in mixtures [N2-F2]. Forbs are **herbaceous, broadleaf plants**, not all of which are legumes, and they can add diversity and have **deep roots** that absorb minerals differently than grasses and legumes [N2-F2].

These morphological differences matter for classification because they create different mixture architectures. Taller species can shade shorter ones, altering light capture and competition; dense canopies can change resource distribution; and different root systems can affect nutrient cycling and belowground competition [N1-R2]. The evidence also shows that morphology is used in practical mixture design, with decisions about **species, genotype, sowing proportion, plant arrangement, and sowing date** shaping the final mixture [N1-F1].

## 2) Phenological classification: timing, sequences, and temporal niches

Phenological classification is based on the timing of life-cycle events. The evidence explicitly identifies **emergence timing, flowering timing, maturity timing, growth duration, and harvesting time** as key phenological traits [N1-R2]. It also notes that phenological phases are **stages in a plant’s life cycle and development**, such as **budding, flowering, fruit set, and ripening** [N3-F3]. This means phenological classification is about how species unfold over time, not just their static form.

In mixtures, emergence, flowering, and maturity timing differ among components. Some species may **emerge earlier, flower later, and mature more quickly** than others, creating distinct developmental sequences within the mixture [N1-R2]. The evidence also links phenological classification to **temporal niche**, showing that species with different phenological sequences occupy different parts of the growing season and can therefore reduce competition [N5-R3]. This is important because resource capture depends on when plants are active: sunlight, water, and nutrients are captured at different times by different species [N5-R3][N5-R4].

Phenological classification is further supported by remote sensing and model-based approaches. The evidence shows that **satellite-derived crop phenology** can improve classification, and that **phenology-based methods** are used to identify crop types [N5-R4][N5-R5]. These approaches emphasize that phenological information is not just descriptive; it is predictive and operational. A mixture with components that flower and mature at different times can therefore be classified as having a broader temporal niche, which may improve resource capture and reduce competition [N5-R3][N5-R4].

## 3) Classification systems and terminology: definitions and operationalization

Different sources define crop mixtures in subtly different ways, which is important for classification. The evidence indicates that **annual crop mixtures** are defined as **within-field mixtures of at least two annual crop species**, or **genotypes of the same species** [N1-F1]. This distinction matters because it separates **species-level mixtures** from **genotype-level mixtures**. It also shows that the term “mixtures” can encompass both **intercropping** and **cultivar mixtures**, although the review itself uses “annual crop mixtures” as the more precise category [N1-F1][N7-R2].

Terminology helps distinguish the three main concepts:
- **Mixtures** refer broadly to combinations of species or genotypes in the field [N1-F1].
- **Intercropping** is used more generally in some sources, but the evidence frames “annual crop mixtures” as the preferred term for within-field mixtures of species or genotypes [N1-F1][N7-R2].
- **Cultivar mixtures** are a subset of mixtures, referring to combinations of genotypes within a species [N7-R2].

Morphological and phenological heterogeneity is operationalized in classification through explicit traits and sequences. Morphological heterogeneity is tied to **plant height, canopy structure, and root architecture** [N1-R2], while phenological heterogeneity is tied to **emergence timing, flowering timing, maturity timing, growth duration, and phenological phases** [N1-R2][N3-F3]. The evidence also shows that classification is based on a **double gradient** of phenological and morphological heterogeneity [N1-R1][N1-F1]. In other words, mixtures are not classified by a single trait alone; they are classified by how their components differ in both form and timing.

This operationalization is increasingly supported by remote sensing and modeling. The evidence shows that crop classification can be improved by integrating **phenological information** and that **phenology-based approaches** are used to identify crop types [N5-R4][N5-R5]. It also notes that landscape heterogeneity and spectral-temporal profiles are used in crop classification systems, showing that classification is not only taxonomic but also performance-oriented [N7-R1][N7-R4]. The cultivar-related evidence further clarifies that **homogeneity and heterogeneity** refer to genetic and phenotypic relationships among plants in a cultivar, and that a cultivar is homogeneous by definition [N7-R5]. This helps distinguish cultivar mixtures from species mixtures: the former may be homogeneous at the cultivar level but heterogeneous at the mixture level, whereas the latter is defined by species-level diversity [N7-R5].

## 4) Performance and practical implications

Morphology and phenology jointly predict competition and yield by shaping how species occupy space and time. The evidence states that crop mixtures are classified based on a **double gradient of phenological and morphological heterogeneity**, which is directly tied to mixture functioning [N1-R1][N1-F1]. Morphological differences such as plant height, canopy structure, and root architecture influence competition by altering **light interception, resource capture, and root-space occupation** [N1-R2]. Phenological differences such as emergence, flowering, maturity timing, and growth duration determine how species interact temporally, affecting **resource availability and competition intensity** [N1-R2][N3-F3]. Together, these traits are used to identify plant traits involved in mixture performance and to quantify the relative contribution of **niche complementarity, facilitation, competition, and plasticity** [N1-F1].

The evidence also shows that certain mixture types are associated with greater stability or productivity. **Wheat mixtures** demonstrated both mid-component and better-component overyielding, with stronger effects under low-input conditions [N4-R1]. **Cultivar mixtures** increased crop yields and temporal yield stability globally, and **varietal mixtures** stabilized productivity even when environmental conditions and stresses were not predicted [N4-R2][N4-R3]. A meta-analysis found that cultivar mixtures improved **resource-use efficiency** and reduced **disease severity** [N4-R2]. The evidence further indicates that **multifaceted functional diversity** improves multifaceted crop yield, reinforcing the idea that mixture composition matters for both **biomass and grain yield** [N4-R4]. However, the evidence also notes that performance depends on the specific combination and arrangement of species, genotypes, and management practices [N1-F1], so classification systems must account for more than just species identity.

In agronomy and farm practice, classification systems are used to **design mixtures, manage them, and integrate them into larger scales**. The review states that crop modeling is used to address issues related to both **crop mixture management** and the **integration of mixtures into larger scales such as rotation** [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that modeling helps identify plant traits involved in mixture performance and quantify ecological processes [N1-F1]. This means classification systems are operationalized in practice through decisions about **species selection, sowing proportion, plant arrangement, sowing date, and management timing** [N1-F1]. The evidence on crop classification also shows that **phenological information improves remote sensing-based classification**, and that temporal changes in crop phenology help achieve better classifications [N5-R4][N5-R5]. This implies that farmers and agronomists use classification systems not only to identify mixtures but also to schedule planting, harvesting, and interventions more effectively [N5-R4][N5-R5].

## 5) Integrated conclusion

Annual crop mixtures are classified by morphological and phenological heterogeneity because these traits determine how species occupy space, compete, and capture resources over time. Morphological classification uses **plant height, canopy structure, and root architecture** to distinguish legumes, cereals, grasses, and forbs [N1-R2][N2-F2]. Phenological classification uses **emergence timing, flowering timing, maturity timing, growth duration, and phenological phases** to distinguish components by their temporal sequences [N1-R2][N3-F3]. These two dimensions are combined into a **double gradient of phenological and morphological heterogeneity**, which is the basis for mixture classification and performance analysis [N1-R1][N1-F1].

Classification systems are also shaped by terminology. Different sources define **mixtures**, **intercropping**, and **cultivar mixtures** differently, but the evidence supports a practical distinction between species-level mixtures and genotype-level mixtures [N1-F1][N7-R2]. Morphological and phenological heterogeneity are operationalized through observable traits and sequences, and they are increasingly supported by remote sensing and modeling approaches that integrate phenological and morphological information [N5-R4][N5-R5][N7-R1][N7-R4]. Finally, these classification systems have clear practical implications: mixtures with greater heterogeneity can be more stable and productive, especially under low-input or unpredictable conditions [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3]. In practice, this means classification is not just a taxonomy; it is a way of designing, managing, and optimizing crop mixtures for sustainable and resilient farming.
